questions.questionText: Why do the lessons ask for WSL2 and Ubuntu, rather than plain Windows PowerShell?
questions.explanation:
The lessons use Linux commands such as `source .venv/bin/activate`. Inside Ubuntu they run unchanged, with no Windows-specific variants.

(A) Python runs fine on Windows. The issue is that the lessons' commands are written for Linux.

(C) The page's reason is that the commands match the lessons, not speed.

options.optionText: Python cannot run on Windows at all
WSL2 runs a real Linux, so the lesson commands work exactly as written
Ubuntu runs the AI models faster than Windows does

questions.questionText: You ran `source .venv/bin/activate` in one Ubuntu terminal. You open a second terminal, and a script fails with `ModuleNotFoundError` for a package you installed. What is the likeliest cause?
questions.explanation:
Activation applies to one terminal only. The page says to run the activate command in every new terminal.

(B) The folder is shared, but a terminal uses it only after activation. A new terminal needs the activate command too.

(C) Packages installed in Ubuntu are used by Ubuntu. Windows is not involved in this error.

options.optionText: The second terminal did not activate the venv, so Python is not using the environment that has the package
The venv folder is shared by every terminal, so the package install must have failed
Packages installed in Ubuntu can only be used from Windows

questions.questionText: Why does the page tell you to keep projects in `~/` rather than under `/mnt/c`?
questions.explanation:
The page says file access under `/mnt/c` is far slower. Under `~/` it is far faster, and VS Code and Explorer can still open the folder.

(A) Linux can read `/mnt/c`. The problem is speed, not access.

(B) You can write to `/mnt/c`. It is just much slower across the Windows boundary.

options.optionText: Linux cannot read Windows folders at all
The `/mnt/c` folder is read-only inside Ubuntu
File access across the Windows boundary is much slower, which hurts `pip install` and git
